Heaps (Theory Video).theory: A binary heap is a complete tree stored in an array: children of i are 2*i+1 and 2*i+2; parent is (i-1)/2. Min-heap parent<=children makes root smallest but does NOT sort the whole array. Sift-down restores order after replacing a root; sift-up after appending a leaf. Bottom-up heap construction is O(n), since most nodes sit near the leaves. PriorityQueue is a Java 8 min-heap by default. Use Collections.reverseOrder for a max-heap. Its iterator is not sorted; poll repeatedly to obtain sorted priorities. Offer/poll take O(log n), peek O(1).

Heapify Algorithm.problem: Build a min heap in place. down(a,i,n,min) is also reusable when both child subtrees are already heaps.
Heapify Algorithm.approach: Visit internal nodes bottom-up. Sift each violating node toward the smaller/larger child until its subtree obeys heap order; child subtrees were already fixed.
Heapify Algorithm.complexity: O(n) build time, O(log n) per sift-down, O(1) auxiliary space.
Heapify Algorithm.trace: At root 3 of [3,1,2], min-heap down swaps with 1, giving [1,3,2].
Heapify Algorithm.pitfalls: A heap array is not fully sorted. Calling down only at root does not fix arbitrary unsorted children.

Implement Min Heap.problem: Resizable int min heap, supporting offer,peek,poll,isEmpty. Empty peek/poll throws.
Implement Min Heap.approach: Offer appends and sifts up while beating parent. Poll removes root, places last at root, then sifts down to the better child. Only one root-to-leaf path can violate order after each operation.
Implement Min Heap.complexity: O(log n) offer/poll, O(1) peek; O(n) stored values, O(1) auxiliary state.
Implement Min Heap.trace: Insert 3 then 1 then 2; root reflects the current extremum. Repeated poll emits priority order.
Implement Min Heap.pitfalls: No comparator subtraction is used, so extreme int values are safe. ArrayList stores boxed integers.

Check if an array represents a min heap.problem: Check min-heap order on a complete array representation.
Check if an array represents a min heap.approach: Every nonroot node must be no smaller than its parent. This local relation along paths makes the root a global minimum.
Check if an array represents a min heap.pitfalls: Sortedness is sufficient but not necessary for heap order. Empty/singleton arrays are heaps.

Convert Min Heap to Max Heap.problem: Build a max heap in place. down(a,i,n,min) is also reusable when both child subtrees are already heaps.
Convert Min Heap to Max Heap.approach: Visit internal nodes bottom-up. Sift each violating node toward the smaller/larger child until its subtree obeys heap order; child subtrees were already fixed.
Convert Min Heap to Max Heap.complexity: O(n) build time, O(log n) per sift-down, O(1) auxiliary space.
Convert Min Heap to Max Heap.trace: At root 3 of [3,1,2], min-heap down swaps with 1, giving [1,3,2].
Convert Min Heap to Max Heap.pitfalls: A heap array is not fully sorted. Calling down only at root does not fix arbitrary unsorted children.

Heap Sort.problem: Sort ascending in place with a max heap.
Heap Sort.approach: Swap the maximum root to the last active position, shrink the active heap, and restore root order. Settled suffix is sorted and never revisited.
Heap Sort.complexity: O(n log n) time; O(1) space; not stable.
Heap Sort.trace: Heap [4,2,3,1] puts 4 last, then 3,2,1 settle in sequence.
Heap Sort.pitfalls: Pass the active prefix length to down; including the sorted suffix would undo progress.

K-th Largest element in an array.problem: Return ONE-based kth largest entry; duplicates count individually.
K-th Largest element in an array.approach: Retain the largest k values in a min-heap; whenever size exceeds k, discard its smallest. Heap root is the smallest of the largest k.
K-th Largest element in an array.trace: For k=2, final retained values are 5 and 6; root is 5.
K-th Largest element in an array.pitfalls: Validate k before peek. kth distinct largest is a different contract.
K-th Largest element in an array.alternatives: Sort in O(n log n); randomized quickselect has expected O(n) time but worst O(n²).

Kth largest element in a stream of runni.problem: Track kth largest after each inserted value; return empty until k values have arrived.
Kth largest element in a stream of runni.approach: Maintain exactly the same largest-k min-heap invariant as batch selection; historical values below the threshold can be discarded permanently.
Kth largest element in a stream of runni.complexity: O(log k) per update, O(k) storage.
Kth largest element in a stream of runni.trace: 3 then 5 retains {3,5}; 4 discards 3, leaving {4,5} and answer 4.
Kth largest element in a stream of runni.pitfalls: A heap with fewer than k values cannot answer kth rank; OptionalInt makes that explicit.

Sort K sorted array.problem: Every value is at most k positions from its final sorted location. Sort in place.
Sort K sorted array.approach: The next smallest value must lie in the next k+1 unread/queued candidates. Poll one, then add the next unread value.
Sort K sorted array.complexity: O(n log(min(n,k+1)+1)) time; O(min(n,k+1)) heap space.
Sort K sorted array.trace: First candidates 3,1,2 emit 1; insert 5, emit 2; insert 4, then emit 3,4,5.
Sort K sorted array.pitfalls: Without the k-displacement promise a small heap may produce an incorrect sort. k=0 expects already sorted input.

Merge K sorted Lists.problem: Merge k disjoint sorted next chains by relinking nodes.
Merge K sorted Lists.approach: Heap holds one front per nonempty chain. The smallest front is globally smallest among remaining entries; after taking it insert only its successor.
Merge K sorted Lists.complexity: O(N log(k+1)) time; O(k) heap space.
Merge K sorted Lists.trace: Heap initially 1,2,3; polling 1 inserts 4, then polling 2 inserts 5.
Merge K sorted Lists.pitfalls: Shared nodes or cycles violate the contract and could duplicate nodes or create loops.

Replace Elements by Their Rank.problem: Dense ranks start at one; equal values share rank, larger distinct values have larger rank.
Replace Elements by Their Rank.approach: Sort values, assign a new rank only on the first occurrence of a distinct value, then map original positions.
Replace Elements by Their Rank.complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) space.
Replace Elements by Their Rank.pitfalls: Rank is based on distinct values, not original indices. Input remains unchanged.

Task Scheduler.problem: Unit tasks A..Z, repeated same task needs at least cooldown intervening time units. Return minimum total including idle.
Task Scheduler.approach: The most frequent tasks force max-1 frames of length cooldown+1 plus the tied maximum tasks at the tail. If other tasks fill more than this lower bound, total task count dominates; arranging tasks in those frames achieves it.
Task Scheduler.trace: A B idle A B idle A B uses eight units for cooldown two.
Task Scheduler.pitfalls: Idle contributes time but not tasks. Empty input returns zero via max(total,frameBound).

Hand of Straights.problem: Partition all cards into groups of exactly group consecutive integer values, counting duplicates.
Hand of Straights.approach: The smallest remaining card must start some group: nothing smaller remains to precede it. Remove one of each required consecutive value, repeat.
Hand of Straights.complexity: O(n log u) time; O(u) space.
Hand of Straights.pitfalls: Check total divisibility first; value arithmetic uses long to reject range overflow.

Design Twitter.problem: In-memory post/follow/unfollow/feed API. Feed includes own posts and followed users, newest first, limited to ten.
Design Twitter.approach: Assign a monotone timestamp per post. For a feed scan eligible histories retaining the newest ten in a min-heap, then reverse their extracted order.
Design Twitter.complexity: O(1) amortized post/follow/unfollow with hash maps; O(H log 10) feed time for H eligible historical posts; O(total posts+follow edges) stored state.
Design Twitter.trace: User 1 sees own tweet 5 and followed user 2's newer 6; after unfollow only 5 remains.
Design Twitter.pitfalls: Self-follow is harmless because feed users form a set. This reference prioritizes clarity; a k-way heap over each user's last post reduces feed work to O(followees+10 log followees).

Minimum Cost to Connect Sticks.problem: Joining two nonnegative stick lengths costs their sum and creates one new stick; minimize total.
Minimum Cost to Connect Sticks.approach: Always merge the two shortest. The optimal merge-tree exchange argument places the two smallest leaves deepest as siblings; collapsing them reduces to the same smaller problem.
Minimum Cost to Connect Sticks.complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) heap space.
Minimum Cost to Connect Sticks.pitfalls: Zero/singleton input costs zero. Use long for joined lengths and cost; extremely large aggregate cost may require BigInteger.

Maximum Sum Combination.problem: Return the k largest pair sums a[i]+b[j], counting distinct index pairs even if sums repeat.
Maximum Sum Combination.approach: Sorted arrays form a monotone sum grid. Begin at its largest corner, pop the largest candidate and add its lower-index neighbors. The frontier contains the next possible largest values; a set prevents revisiting pairs.
Maximum Sum Combination.complexity: O(n log n+m log m+k log(k+1)) time; O(n+m+k) space.
Maximum Sum Combination.pitfalls: Deduplicate coordinate pairs, not sums. Validate k against number of possible pairs.

Find Median from Data Stream.problem: After each insertion return the median of all seen values; no value exists before the first insertion.
Find Median from Data Stream.approach: Max-heap low contains the smaller half; min-heap high the larger. Keep low the same size or one larger and every low value<=every high value. Middle value(s) are the roots.
Find Median from Data Stream.complexity: O(log n) insertion, O(1) median; O(n) storage.
Find Median from Data Stream.trace: After 1,2 roots are 1 and 2 ->1.5; after 3 low root 2 ->2.
Find Median from Data Stream.pitfalls: Widen before averaging roots to avoid int overflow. Heap iterators do not give sorted order.

Top K Frequent Elements.problem: Return k distinct values ranked by descending frequency then ascending value.
Top K Frequent Elements.approach: Count once and sort distinct keys using the stated tie comparator. Take the first k.
Top K Frequent Elements.complexity: Expected O(n+u log u) time; O(u) space.
Top K Frequent Elements.pitfalls: k<=distinct count, not input length. For large u and small k use a size-k heap in O(n+u log k), or frequency buckets.
